steps.prompt: Want ONE consistent voice across every track you make?
steps.sub: Each generation gives you a different singer. To build a brand, you need the SAME voice every time. By the end you'll understand voice conversion (RVC): train one voice, then stamp it onto any vocal you generate.

steps.prompt: Your problem: every track you generate has a different-sounding singer. What fixes it?

options.t: Generate more tracks until two happen to match by luck.
Train ONE voice model, then convert every generated vocal to that same voice.
Turn off vocals entirely and only make instrumentals.

steps.why: Voice conversion (RVC) lets you train a single target voice once, then apply it to any vocal — so every track sings in your signature voice. Hoping two random takes match is hopeless, and dropping vocals throws away the whole point. Train once, reuse everywhere.
hints: You want the SAME voice every time. Random generation can't promise that.
What if you could 'convert' any vocal to a single fixed voice you trained?

steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the whole idea in four pieces.

cards.b: The one voice you want to own — your AI singer's identity.
Feed clean samples of that target voice so the model learns its timbre.
Any generated vocal — the WORDS and melody you want sung.
Re-voice the source so it keeps the notes/words but sounds like your target.

steps.prompt: When you convert a vocal with RVC, what is KEPT and what is REPLACED?
steps.sub: This is the core of how it works.

options.t: It keeps the melody and words, and replaces the voice's identity (timbre).
It keeps the voice and replaces the lyrics with new ones.
It replaces everything — melody, words and voice all change.

steps.why: Voice conversion preserves the performance — the notes sung and the words — and swaps only the timbre (who it sounds like). That's exactly why it's powerful: you generate any vocal you like, then stamp your singer's identity on top without losing the song.
hints: The word is voice CONVERSION — what's being converted, the song or the singer?
You generated the melody and lyrics already. You only want to change WHO sings them.

steps.prompt: Training a good voice model: helpful or harmful?
steps.sub: Tap each item, then drop it in the right bin.

items.t: Clean, dry vocal samples of ONE consistent voice
Background music and noise mixed into the samples
Enough total minutes to cover the voice's range
A mix of three different people's voices in one dataset
Consistent recording quality across all clips

hints: You're teaching the model ONE identity. What blurs that identity?
Noise and multiple speakers confuse the model about who it's learning.

steps.prompt: Tap the steps to build and use your AI singer.
steps.sub: From zero to a converted track in your own voice.
chips: Generate a vocal track (the words + melody you want)
Collect clean samples of your target voice
Train the RVC voice model on those samples
Convert the generated vocal to your trained voice
hints: Before you can train, you need the samples to train ON.
Conversion is the final step — it needs both a trained voice AND a vocal to convert.

steps.prompt: True or false — about your AI singer.
steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check.

statements.t: You train the voice once, then reuse it across many future tracks.
statements.why: Right — that's the payoff. One training run gives you a reusable voice you can stamp onto every new vocal, building a consistent identity.

statements.t: Voice conversion writes new lyrics for you.
statements.why: No — RVC changes WHO sings, not WHAT is sung. The words come from the source vocal you generated; conversion only swaps the timbre.

statements.t: Noisy, music-bleeding samples make a cleaner trained voice.
statements.why: No — noise and background music confuse the model. Clean, dry, single-voice samples produce a cleaner, more faithful trained voice.

statements.t: Using a consistent AI singer helps you build a recognizable brand.
statements.why: Yes — a signature voice across all your tracks makes your catalog instantly recognizable, just like a real artist's voice does.

hints: Remember what conversion keeps (the song) vs. swaps (the voice).
Garbage in, garbage out — what kind of samples train a clean voice?

steps.prompt: Walk a real 'build my singer' run.
steps.sub: Pick the next move at each step. The log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Make two different songs that BOTH sing in your one signature voice.

turns.situation: You've decided on a target voice you want to own. You have nothing trained yet.
turns.q: What's the first thing RVC needs?
options: Clean, dry samples of that one target voice
A noisy live recording with a crowd
turns.log: 📚 Collect clean samples of the target voice

turns.situation: You've gathered good samples of a single, consistent voice.
turns.q: What do you do with them?
options: Train the RVC voice model on them
Convert them to a random voice
Delete half of them at random

turns.situation: Your voice model is trained. You generate Song A (a pop hook, default singer).
turns.q: How do you make Song A sing in YOUR voice?
options: Convert Song A's vocal to your trained voice
Re-train the model on Song A
turns.log: 🔁 Convert Song A → your signature voice

turns.situation: Now you generate Song B (a totally different ballad, different default singer).
turns.q: Do you need to train again for Song B?
options: No — reuse the same trained voice, just convert Song B too
Yes — train a whole new model
No — Song B can't use the voice
turns.log: 🔁 Convert Song B → same voice · ✅ consistent singer

hints: The order is: samples → train → generate → convert.
Training is a one-time cost. Once trained, you just keep CONVERTING new vocals.

steps.prompt: Tap ALL the true statements about voice conversion (RVC).
steps.sub: Some are real; some are myths. Pick only the real ones.
chips: It gives you ONE consistent voice across tracks
It keeps the song, swaps the timbre
It writes the lyrics for you
It needs noisy samples to work
steps.why: RVC gives you a reusable, consistent voice: train once on clean single-voice samples, then convert any generated vocal — keeping the words and melody while swapping the timbre. It does NOT write lyrics (those come from the source vocal) and noisy samples hurt, not help.
